ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r1.claim: He says spending for God steadies part of oneself, while giving both wealth and life in God's path steadies all of it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r10.claim: The garden parable contrasts with the first parable: the stone does not benefit from rain.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r2.claim: The self itself moves and steadies the giver through its faith and expectation of abundant reward.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r4.claim: The high ground is singled out for its good trees and abundant fruit.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r5.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r5.claim: His poem depicts a raised garden between dry heights and thirsty lowlands, watered by itself and bearing fruit at different levels.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r6.claim: He explains rabwa as elevated land without flowing rivers; the author limits this to the particular garden because it receives rain.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r7.claim: The garden depends on rain rather than running water, as was familiar in Arabia.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r8.speaker: الرازي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r8.claim: He objects that gardens on high ground lack river water and face winds, while hollows collect water; he instead reads rabwa as fertile earth swelling under rain.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r9.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r9.claim: Hasan had already explained rabwa as level ground that does not rise above the water.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r1.claim: He rejects al-Tabari's interpretation of رياض الحزن as gardens of elevated ground; it means gardens of Najd, called al-Hazn.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r10.claim: Ḍiʿfayn is a circumstantial accusative, not a second object; taking آتت to mean produced with one object lacks support in Arabic usage.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r11.claim: Fruit is attached to the garden by relation, not ownership; al-ḥamza in الأكل marks the thing eaten.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r12.speaker: الحرميان وأبو عمرو
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r12.claim: They read ukul with ḍamma on hamza and sukūn on kāf in the described feminine annexation contexts; Abu Amr also transmits a distinction by annexed noun.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r13.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r13.claim: The remaining readers use the heavier vocalization for ukul.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r2.claim: Najd's gardens are praised because their vegetation is more fragrant and their air cooler and finer than Tihama's.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r3.speaker: ابن عامر وعاصم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r3.claim: They read rabwa with fatḥa on rāʾ, while the other five canonical readers use ḍamma; the same difference occurs at قد أفلح.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r4.claim: He reads rabwa with kasra on rāʾ.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r5.speaker: أبو جعفر وأبو عبد الرحمن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r5.claim: They read برباوة on the pattern of كراهة.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r6.speaker: أبو الأشهب العقيلي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r6.claim: He reads برباوة on the pattern of رسالة.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r7.claim: أصابها وابل is an adjectival clause for garden, following the fixed location description; it may instead be a circumstantial clause.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r8.claim: The wording first gives the lasting feature of being on a high place, then the incidental event of rain; its ordering differs from the stone parable.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p668/r9.claim: آتت means gave, with its recipient omitted; the first object is owner or people and أكل means the edible fruit.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r1.claim: Ḍiʿfayn may mean twice the normal yield because of rain and the high place, twice other land, or fourfold if a double is taken as two times.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r10.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r10.claim: He compares sincere spenders to the garden, and abundant or modest spending to heavy rain or dew; either is accepted when seeking God's face and exerting one's capacity.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r2.speaker: أبو مسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r2.claim: He says the garden yields three times as much; Taj al-Qurra rejects this as having no basis in Arabic and says the doubled yield is one harvest.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r3.speaker: عكرمة وعطاء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r3.claim: They interpret doubled fruit as two harvests in one year.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r4.claim: He suggests ḍiʿfayn can express multiplication rather than exactly twice one yield, meaning many successive multiples, matching the manyfold reward for good deeds.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r5.speaker: ابن عيسى
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r5.claim: He supplies an omitted clause after the conditional: if rain does not strike it, as in the poetic example where لم تلدني means she did not happen to bear me.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r6.claim: On one reading, dew substitutes for heavy rain and the fertile land still yields doubled fruit despite less rainfall.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r7.speaker: الماوردي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r7.claim: Alternatively, dew yields less than heavy rain, but still gives some yield and benefit.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r8.claim: He rejects proposed fronting and postponement as unnecessary and says the Qur'an should not be assigned a poetic license.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r9.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p669/r9.claim: He identifies the parable's land as Egypt, which thrives without rain and doubles its yield with rain.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r1.speaker: الماوردي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r1.claim: He compares abundant charity to rain-fed crops and modest charity to dew-fed crops, so a little good should not be abandoned when one cannot give much.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r2.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r2.claim: He compares the growth of sincere gifts, which God nurtures like young livestock, to vegetation on the fertile raised garden, unlike bare stone.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r3.speaker: ابن الجوزي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r3.claim: He says the sincere believer's expenditure never fails: dew makes the garden good and heavy rain doubles it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r4.claim: He parses فطل as the conditional answer with an omitted clause, offering several viable ellipses; the simplest remove one part of a clause.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r5.claim: A present verb after fa requires an implicit subject, as in the cited verse, so that analysis also needs an omitted clause.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r6.claim: A poetic parallel uses a verbless noun phrase after the condition, like the parsing of فطل.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r7.speaker: الزهري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r7.claim: He reads بصير with yāʾ, apparently referring to hypocrites, though the author allows a general reference to everyone.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p670/r8.claim: The majority read بصير with address to the audience; the shift of address highlights that God knows every deed and intention, promising reward and warning.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r1.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r1.claim: تثبيتا can be the verbal noun of intransitive تثبت, used in place of التثبت; verbal nouns substitute for one another, as in 73:8, and a reading تثبتا supports this.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r2.speaker: ابن رواحة
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r2.claim: Ibn Rawāḥa’s line uses تثبيت with ثبت الله and supports the transitive verb’s verbal-noun usage.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r3.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r3.claim: Al-Shaykh rejects substitution unless the corresponding verb is explicitly stated first; otherwise a verbal noun keeps its original verb’s meaning.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r4.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r4.claim: He instead distinguishes intransitive ثبت, ‘become firm,’ from causative ثبّت, ‘make firm.’

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains partitive من as partial self-commitment: spending wealth steadies part of oneself, while giving life and wealth steadies the whole self.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r6.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r6.claim: The apparent meaning is that believers’ own faith steadies and moves them to spend; the author therefore favors construing تثبيت as attributed in meaning to themselves.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#2/r7.claim: If تثبيت is attributed to the spenders, من is an accusative partitive attached to the verbal noun; if attributed semantically to themselves, من also modifies تثبيتا.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r1.speaker: الخليل
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r1.claim: ربوة is an elevated, fertile tract, derived from ربا يربو, ‘rise’; al-Suddī’s interpretation as low-lying land is wrong.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r2.claim: Forms include ربوة and رباوة with three vowelings, plus رابية; the cited poem witnesses روابيه.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r3.speaker: ابن عامر وعاصم
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r3.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim read ربوة with fatḥa; the others use ḍamma.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r4.speaker: الأخفش
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r4.claim: Al-Akhfash prefers ḍamma because the plural رباً points to a singular with ḍamma, like برمة/برم and صورة/صور.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads ربوة with kasra.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r6.speaker: الأشهب العقيلي وأبو جعفر
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#3/r6.claim: Al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī reads رياوة and Abū Jaʿfar reads رباوة, alongside other dialect forms.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r1.claim: أصابها وابل may be a second adjective of جنة; preferred order puts the stable location before the temporary rain event and commonly places a prepositional phrase before a clause.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r2.claim: It may instead modify ربوة, since the garden is part of the elevated tract.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r3.claim: A third analysis makes the clause circumstantial from the implicit pronoun inside the prepositional phrase describing the garden.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#4/r4.claim: A fourth analysis makes it circumstantial from جنة, now specified by its adjective, with قد understood.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r1.claim: آتت normally takes two objects, with صاحبها or أهلها omitted as first because the point is what the garden yields and its owner is implied; أكلها is second and ضعفين circumstantial.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r2.claim: Treating ضعفين as the second object is a slip and an error.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r3.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r3.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ analyzes آتت as ‘produced,’ making it a one-object verb; al-Shaykh says that meaning is not known in Arabic, so attributing giving to a garden is metaphorical.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r4.speaker: نافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r4.claim: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and Abū ʿAmr read أكلها with ḍamma hamza and still kāf for feminine annexations; Abū ʿAmr’s stated exception concerns masculine or non-pronominal annexations.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#5/r5.claim: Other readers double the kāf generally; أكل with ḍamma means food and with fatḥa means eating, and it is annexed to the garden as its place or cause.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r1.speaker: المبرد
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r1.claim: After conditional fa, the omitted completion may be a predicate: طل is subject of ‘dew falls on it’; an indefinite subject is licensed in a conditional answer.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r2.claim: A second parse makes طل predicate of an omitted subject: ‘what falls on it is dew.’

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r3.claim: A third, clearest parse makes طل the subject of an omitted verb: ‘dew then falls on it.’

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r4.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r4.claim: Al-Shaykh argues that the third parse deletes the answer clause while retaining one constituent; a present verb after answer-fa needs an omitted subject, as in 5:95.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r5.claim: The author disputes that present-tense verbs after answer-fa necessarily require an implicit subject.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r6.speaker: امرؤ القيس
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r6.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays’s phrase فمعزى can be analyzed by the same three parses as فطل.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r7.claim: The proposed inversion that moves fruit-yielding after the conditional is unnecessary: the meaning works already, and normal order is preferred absent necessity.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r8.speaker: مجاهد
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r8.claim: Mujāhid glosses طل as dew; the author calls this figurative. طل is fine droplets; طلّه الندى and أطله are used, and its plural is طلال.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#6/r9.claim: The cited line ولما نزلنا منزلا طله الندى witnesses the verb usage طله.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#7/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#7/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#7/r1.claim: The majority’s خطاب تعلمون shifts from third-person narration to direct address, encouraging sincere spending and deterring ostentation and reputation-seeking.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265#7/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#7/r2.speaker: الزهري
SAMIN-DURR:2:265#7/r2.claim: Al-Zuhrī reads يعلمون in the third person, referring either to the spenders or generally to all people, with spenders included first.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r1.claim: The comparison through كمثل حبة follows the same grammatical analyses as the parable in 2:261.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r2.speaker: الجحدري
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r2.claim: Al-Jaḥdarī reads كمثل حبة, with unpointed ḥāʾ and bāʾ.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r3.claim: ابتغاء may be a causal accusative or a circumstantial accusative; تثبيتا coordinates with it under either parse.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r4.speaker: ابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects ابتغاء as causal because تثبيتا is coordinated with it and spending is not done for the sake of confirmation.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r5.speaker: مكي
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r5.claim: Makkī permits ابتغاء as causal, a view Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls rejected.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r6.claim: If تثبيتا means securing God’s reward from themselves, that reward can motivate spending; if it means making their deeds sincere, a causal reading is unclear.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r7.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r7.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ supplies the object as their deeds through sincere intention, and also allows من أنفسهم to function as the object with من meaning ل.

SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:265/r8.claim: من أنفسهم has two analyses: an object through shifted preposition, or an adjective of تثبيتا; تثبيت itself may be transitive or intransitive.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#2/r1.claim: Wābil is heavy rain, ukul is fruit, and ḍiʿfayn means twice the yield compared with other gardens.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#2/r2.speaker: الضحاك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#2/r2.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says ṭall is drizzle, a gentle rain; the high garden is sustained by either heavy rain or drizzle, just as a believer's work is never wasted but accepted and multiplied according to the person's deeds.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#2/r3.claim: God sees everything His servants do, and none of their deeds is hidden from Him.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r1.claim: Believers who give seeking God's pleasure do so with conviction that He will reward them fully; this resembles the authenticated report about fasting Ramadan in faith and seeking reward.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r2.speaker: الشعبي، قتادة، أبو صالح، ابن زيد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r2.claim: Al-Shaʿbī interprets the phrase as affirmation and certainty; Qatāda, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and Ibn Zayd agree, and Ibn Jarīr selects this view.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r3.speaker: مجاهد، الحسن
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r3.claim: Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan instead say that donors carefully establish where to place their charity.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r4.speaker: الجمهور، ابن عباس، الضحاك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r4.claim: Most commentators define a rabwa as level ground at an elevated place; Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk add that streams run there.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r5.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695/r5.claim: Ibn Jarīr notes three dialectal and recitational forms of rabwa: with ḍamma, common in Medina, the Ḥijāz, and Iraq; fatḥa, used by some Syrians and Kūfans and attributed to Tamīm; and kasra, reported as Ibn ʿAbbās's reading.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p517/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p517/r8.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p517/r8.claim: The sincere garden parable is paired by contrast with the showy spender in this verse and by thematic correspondence with the earlier good-spending parable.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r1.claim: The sincere spenders seek God's pleasure without worldly or egoistic motives or other defects that would corrupt the deed; marḍāt suggests repeated, enduring satisfaction.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r2.claim: The form marḍāt conveys satisfaction that recurs and persists.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r3.claim: Self-fortification means carefully repairing and purifying one's deeds through patience and restraint; making the soul yield in spending wealth, its close companion, eases other worship, while indulging it strengthens appetite for base desires.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r4.claim: The preposition min is partitive and governs the self as an object, as in the expression to soften someone with one's affection or stir them with one's energy.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r5.claim: The grain parable represents spending in God's path, while the enduring orchard represents spending from the motive of seeking God's pleasure across every good path.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r6.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r6.claim: A garden on a ridge receives sunlight and pollinating winds; a valley garden is less alive because such winds pass over it, and wind is described as the Breath of the All-Merciful.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r7.claim: The author's preferred sense of double yield is four times the ordinary crop: a double is an amount plus its equal, so two doubles make four, though commentators commonly say twofold.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r8.claim: The parable uses ellipsis by correspondence: the spender named first implies the garden's owner later, while naming the garden implies the omitted expenditure.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r9.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p518/r9.claim: Dew is one subtle stage of rainfall, initially imperceptible; rain progresses from dew to light drizzle, spray, steady rain, downpour, and heavy deluge.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r1.claim: Sincere deeds cannot be invalidated, though weak intentions can diminish them; God sees both outward and inward work, so both should be improved.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r2.claim: The text presents the unconditioned warning before the positive incentive because preventing harm takes priority over seeking benefit, then returns to warn against boasting and ostentation with a clearer image.

DURR-FULL:v2p45/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r10.speaker: الشعبي
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r10.claim: Thabitan min anfusihim means faith and certainty.

DURR-FULL:v2p45/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r11.speaker: أبو صالح
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r11.claim: Thabitan min anfusihim means conviction from within themselves.

DURR-FULL:v2p45/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r12.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r12.claim: Thabitan means carefully considering where to place one's money.

DURR-FULL:v2p45/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r13.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r13.claim: A person intending charity would pause; he proceeded if it was for God and held back if showmanship intruded.

DURR-FULL:v2p45/r15.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r15.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r15.claim: Ibn Abbas recited rabwa with kasra on the ra; rabwa is elevated ground.

DURR-FULL:v2p45/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r7.speaker: الربيع
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r7.claim: The garden parable represents the believer's deed.

DURR-FULL:v2p45/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r8.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r8.claim: Seeking God's pleasure means acting in hope of reward.

DURR-FULL:v2p45/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r9.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v2p45/r9.claim: Those who seek God's pleasure do not seek reputation or show.

DURR-FULL:v2p46/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r1.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r1.claim: A rabwa is level ground that is elevated.

DURR-FULL:v2p46/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r10.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r10.claim: The believer's good deed is never lost, just as the garden yields whether it receives heavy rain or dew.

DURR-FULL:v2p46/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r11.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r11.claim: He identifies the land as Egypt, where dew produces well and heavy rain doubles the yield.

DURR-FULL:v2p46/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r2.claim: A garden on a rabwa stands on high ground where rivers do not flow.

DURR-FULL:v2p46/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r3.speaker: مقاتل
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r3.claim: Wabil means rain striking the garden.

DURR-FULL:v2p46/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r5.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r5.claim: The garden yielded double its usual fruit.

DURR-FULL:v2p46/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r6.speaker: السدي
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r6.claim: As the garden's fruit was doubled, the spender's reward is likewise doubled.

BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r1.claim: Seeking God's pleasure with expenditure stabilizes part of the self against innate love of wealth and reluctance to spend; the soul can be trained despite its natural inclinations.

BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r2.speaker: البوصيري
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r2.claim: The Burda compares the self to a child: if left alone it grows attached to nursing, but if weaned it can be weaned.

BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r3.claim: Neglect strengthens idleness and miserliness; imposing difficult bodily and financial worship brings the self into line and purifies it of acquired habits.

BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r4.claim: The preposition من can mean 'some of,' as in the idiom about shaking some liveliness from one's sleeve.

BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r5.claim: Wealth counts as part of the self because of the soul's intense attachment to it; giving money stabilizes a part of oneself, while giving life and money gives the whole self.

BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r6.speaker: جلال الدين الرومي
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r6.claim: Rumi's verses distinguish giving money from giving one's life for God and say God repays each with the corresponding gift.

BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r7.claim: A second reading takes تثبيتا as making something true and firm: spending confirms faith rooted in the heart and confidence that God rewards good action.

BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r8.claim: On this reading من marks the origin of faith in the heart, as in the cited phrase 'envy from themselves.'

BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p346#2/r9.claim: A garden on a raised hill enjoys gentle air and protection from hail, yielding better-looking trees and sweeter fruit than low ground with stagnant air.

BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r1.claim: The comparison may be distributive: divine favor and standing are the fruit, while large and small donations are heavy and light rain; both increase the result.

BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r2.claim: God sees sincere work and ostentation, so the verse urges sincerity and warns against showing off.

BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r3.claim: A discerning worshipper should seek sincerity and freedom from hidden idolatry, since release from it depends on sincere devotion.

BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r4.speaker: السعدي
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r4.claim: Saʿdī warns that sowing thorns cannot yield flowers, so insincere work will not bear its hoped-for fruit.

BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r5.claim: Pure work is done without wanting anyone to praise its doer; sincerity transforms work and multiplies its reward.

BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r6.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r6.claim: ʿAlī reports from the Prophet that charity speaks five benefits: it grows, is enlarged, turns an enemy into a friend, preserves what would perish, and guards its giver.

BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r7.speaker: مكحول الشامي
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r7.claim: Makḥūl says Hell asks leave to prostrate in gratitude when a believer gives charity, since the gift frees a member of Muḥammad's community from punishment.

BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347#2/r8.claim: He assigns meanings to charity's letters: ṣād repels harm, dāl guides its giver to Paradise, and qāf signifies nearness to God.

BURSEVI:v1p347/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347/r1.claim: Some say a productive garden should stand on level ground; rabwa here means soft, fertile soil that swells and grows after rain.

BURSEVI:v1p347/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347/r10.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347/r10.claim: The parable says sincere, strengthening expenditures are pure and never wasted, though their purity varies with intention, like a garden thriving from good soil and rain.

BURSEVI:v1p347/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347/r2.claim: He supports this soil reading with the description of earth stirring and swelling after rain.

BURSEVI:v1p347/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347/r3.claim: Wābil is heavy rain with large drops and forceful impact; the garden yields its fruit or harvest to its owner or household.

BURSEVI:v1p347/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347/r4.claim: Akl means the garden's fruit and yield, literally something eaten; ātat can also mean brought forth with aklahā as its sole object.

BURSEVI:v1p347/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347/r5.claim: The doubled yield is twice the usual crop because of the heavy rain.

BURSEVI:v1p347/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
BURSEVI:v1p347/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says one year's yield equals what another garden produces in two years, so double means a like amount.

BURSEVI:v1p347/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347/r7.claim: Another interpretation counts four times the usual crop by taking each double as two times the thing itself.

BURSEVI:v1p347/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347/r8.claim: A light drizzle suffices because the soil is excellent and the air mild; sustained drizzle can work like heavy rain.

BURSEVI:v1p347/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p347/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p347/r9.claim: An indefinite noun can begin a clause because it answers a conditional, a recognized license for an indefinite subject.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r1.claim: Spending to seek God’s pleasure means giving in order to obtain His approval.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r2.claim: The phrase strengthening oneself may use min partitivally: spending engages one faculty of the self; giving both wealth and life would engage the whole self.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r3.claim: Alternatively, min is origination and the omitted object is Islam or confirmation of recompense, rooted in the heart; it may also indicate proving sincerity to other believers.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r4.claim: Mujāhid’s reading tabyīnan, ‘making clear,’ supports interpreting the phrase as showing others one’s sincere faith.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r5.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r5.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī takes min to mean li, so the phrase describes steadying oneself for obedience to God; the author finds this plausible.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p35#2/r6.claim: Spending purifies the donor from miserliness and love of wealth, described as a grave disease and root of every sin.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r1.claim: A garden on elevated ground has especially attractive trees and wholesome fruit because its air is mild and does not stagnate densely.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r2.speaker: ابن عامر، عاصم
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r2.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim read rabwa with fatḥ; most read ḍamm, Ibn ʿAbbās reads kasr, and another form is rabāwa.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r3.claim: A variant reads ḥabba, ‘grain,’ instead of janna, ‘garden.’

ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r4.claim: The doubled yield may mean repeated abundance, twice the ordinary crop after heavy rain, four times if ḍiʿf means double, or two harvests in one year.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r5.speaker: أبو عمرو، ابن كثير، نافع
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r5.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Kathīr, and Nāfiʿ read the kāf in akl with sukūn as a lightened pronunciation.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r6.claim: Even light drizzle suffices for a good garden on high ground, so sincere spending never fails to yield reward, though sincerity, effort, love of wealth, and the recipient’s need affect its degree.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r7.claim: The analogy may be composite, matching pure growing expenditure with a pure fruitful garden under either rain, or differentiated, matching the donors and their small or great gifts with garden and rain.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r8.claim: On the composite analysis the common feature is growth joined with purity; on the differentiated analysis, either the expenditure or the donor is the main comparison, and scholars prefer different constructions.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p36/r9.claim: God sees every deed and rewards the sincere while warning the ostentatious giver who seeks the gaze of those whose view cannot help, instead of God’s decisive sight.

ELMALILI:2:265/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:265/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:265/r1.claim: The sincere donor seeks God's pleasure and uses wealth to steady themselves, their deeds, and their companions against corrupt inclinations and instability, making good works a settled habit.

ELMALILI:2:265/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:265/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:265/r2.claim: A garden on a high hill yields twice its usual fruit under a heavy rain; the earlier rain that stripped rock becomes mercy here.

ELMALILI:2:265/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:265/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:265/r3.claim: The garden's doubled yield does not reduce the earlier promise of seven hundredfold; it adds another multiplication.

ELMALILI:2:265/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:265/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:265/r4.claim: Even without a heavy downpour, a light drizzle or slight moisture is enough for the garden to produce its yield.

ELMALILI:2:265/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:265/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:265/r5.claim: Because God sees and knows deeds, donors must avoid showing off and remain sincere in private and public.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r1.claim: The sincere spender's garden is set against the show-off spender's image to make the distance between the ranks vivid and renew praise; a more intricate picture beautifies its subject.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r2.claim: The earlier seed image is simple for swiftly picturing multiplied reward; this garden image is more involved because several favorable features enhance the scene and its analogue.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r3.claim: ابتغاء مرضاة الله and تثبيتا are circumstantial accusatives, meaning seeking God's pleasure and strengthening themselves; تثبيت depicts restraining inner hesitation and stinginess.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p50/r4.claim: Repeated practice of difficult virtues makes them firm habits; spending especially strengthens obedience because wealth is precious, and من marks a figurative partiality among states of the self.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53/r1.claim: The dual ضعفين indicates repetition rather than exactly two, like لبيك: the garden yields multiplied produce in varying measure.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53/r2.claim: Even without heavy rain, light rain yields a lesser crop; sincere spending brings great reward that varies with sincerity and self-strengthening but never disappoints its giver.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r6.speaker: الصادق عليه السلام
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r6.claim: Al-Qummī glosses ṣafwān as a large rock, wābil as rain, tall as nighttime dew on plants, and iʿṣār as winds.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.claim: The connected themes suggest this passage was revealed as one unit: spending grows seven hundredfold or more, sincere giving bears fruit, ostentation and reminders or harm ruin reward, good wealth should be given, the poor detained in God's path are recipients, and the reward is great.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.claim: The passage orders its teaching around purpose (giving for God, not people), manner (without reproach or injury), quality (good rather than bad wealth), recipient (the needy constrained in God's path), and reward.

TABATABAI:2:265-266/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r1.claim: Tathbīt is the self's resolve to keep itself firm in the pure intention it formed; min marks its source, anfus is the agent, and the implied object is the self itself.

TABATABAI:2:265-266/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r2.claim: Rabwa derives from growth and means good elevated land; akl is what is eaten, and tall is weak rain with little effect.

TABATABAI:2:265-266/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r3.claim: The garden parable says sincere spending unfailingly bears good fruit because divine care remains attached to it, though yield varies with the purity of intention and the quality of the rain.

TABATABAI:2:265-266/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r4.claim: God's seeing means He distinguishes differing deeds and rewards without confusing one person's reward with another's.

TABATABAI:2:265/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:265/r1.claim: Seeking God's pleasure means intending His face: for the commanded servant, God's 'face' is His satisfaction with obedience after the command first addresses the servant.

TABATABAI:2:265/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265/r2.speaker: قيل
TABATABAI:2:265/r2.claim: One reported interpretation takes 'stabilizing themselves' to mean assent and certainty.

TABATABAI:2:265/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265/r3.speaker: قيل
TABATABAI:2:265/r3.claim: Another reported interpretation says they carefully decide where to place their money.

TABATABAI:2:265/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265/r4.speaker: قيل
TABATABAI:2:265/r4.claim: A further interpretation says they verify their spending, proceeding if it is for God and withholding if ostentation intrudes.

TABATABAI:2:265/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265/r5.speaker: قيل
TABATABAI:2:265/r5.claim: Another interpretation makes it a resolve of the self to obey God.

TABATABAI:2:265/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265/r6.speaker: قيل
TABATABAI:2:265/r6.claim: Another interpretation is to establish oneself in faith by habituating oneself to give for God's sake.

TABATABAI:2:265/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:265/r7.claim: The author says none of these reported explanations fits the wording without strained interpretation.

TABATABAI:2:265/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:265/r8.claim: The passage first excludes ostentation, which invalidates a deed from the outset, and spending later spoiled by mann or harm; it then describes sincere givers who hold fast to their pure intention.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:265/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:265/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:265/r1.claim: Giving to those in need from faith and sincere inner conviction for God's pleasure yields in proportion to intention, like an orchard protected from harmful winds that bears much in heavy rain and some in drizzle.

QIRAAT-ER:2:265:17#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:265:17#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:265:17#1/r1.claim: Changing fatḥa to ḍamma on rāʾ gives rubwa instead of rabwa; both dialectal forms mean elevated ground.

QIRAAT-ER:2:265:22#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:265:22#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:265:22#1/r1.claim: Sukūn on kāf lightens pronunciation while preserving meaning; both forms are canonical.

STUDYQURAN:2:264/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r10.speaker: IK, Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r10.claim: IK and Ṭ understand giving out of inner confirmation as expressing certainty of faith in the act of giving.

STUDYQURAN:2:264/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r11.speaker: Z
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r11.claim: Z reads inner confirmation as confirmation of God’s Truth or certainty.

STUDYQURAN:2:264/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r12.speaker: Q, R
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r12.claim: Q and R understand the phrase as giving carefully and confirming that charity is placed where it will be used properly.

STUDYQURAN:2:264/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r2.claim: Rain imagery contrasts charity spoiled by bad intention with giving done for God’s pleasure and secure faith.

STUDYQURAN:2:264/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r4.claim: Rain on a fertile garden doubles its yield, symbolizing charity given with the right intention.

STUDYQURAN:2:264/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r5.claim: Even without a downpour, a softer rain lets the garden thrive and bear fruit.

STUDYQURAN:2:264/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r6.speaker: Some commentators
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r6.claim: Some commentators say elevated oases gather rich earth and flourish; because streams do not reach them, rain alone nourishes them.

STUDYQURAN:2:264/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r7.speaker: Others
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r7.claim: Others read bi-rabwah as something that rises, meaning fertile soil from which crops grow upward.

STUDYQURAN:2:264/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r8.speaker: al-Rāzī
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r8.claim: Al-Rāzī argues hills lack streams and face too much wind, while hollows flood; he says level ground is best and prefers a meaning tied to growth.

STUDYQURAN:2:264/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:264/r9.claim: A hadith says God grows a lawfully earned date given in charity until it becomes mountain-sized or larger.
